title: The fine print of banks’ travel insurance changes
full_text:
A dramatic overhaul of travel insurance linked to credit cards has prompted warnings for consumers to double-check the fine print and consider changing providers altogether.
Ahead of the Reserve Bank banning credit card surcharges from October 1, all the major banks have been making significant changes to their rewards program rules, including credit cards’ complimentary travel insurance that cardholders have received for many years.
Canstar data insights director Sally Tindall says it is “no longer a given” that credit card travel insurance policies could provide adequate protection.
“When heading overseas, travel insurance is the second-most important thing to pack with you, after your passport,” Tindall says.
She says cardholders have used the insurance as a free safety net, but many of the new changes were “so extreme that travellers may decide to ditch the credit card policy for a separate one that covers them for a lot more than an unexpected trip to the hospital”.
“You shouldn’t assume the policy you had last year, or even for your last trip, will still provide the same protection now,” she says.
“It’s also worth double-checking what you have to do, if anything, to activate your insurance, as this may have changed recently as well.” Canstar has found all of the big four banks have announced travel insurance changes in recent months. Among the many changes, here are some of the more significant moves.
Commonwealth Bank CBA’s major loyalty program revamp, announced in August, included capping some types of cover and switching insurers from Cover More, owned by Swiss-based Zurich Insurance Group, to Cover Genius, a US global insurance and technology company that operates in 60 countries.
Review websites typically rate Cover Genius below Cover More for customer service, with Trustpilot giving it a “poor” rating from 242 reviews and productreview.com.au rating its XCover subsidiary 2.1 stars out of five from 556 reviews.
Westpac The bank is scaling back complimentary travel card insurance, scrapping cover for trip cancellation, travel delay, vehicle excess and accidental death and luggage for international travellers, leaving only limited medical cover.
Customers who booked a trip or are planning to book a trip between now and October 1 can still get cover under the existing arrangement, even if their trip is at a later date, provided they meet the current eligibility criteria and the trip finishes by September 30 next year.
ANZ The bank is cutting travel insurance altogether for some rewards credit cards, including ANZ Rewards Black and ANZ Rewards Platinum, and paring it back for its frequent-flyer cards. The changes are occurring in December and March.
Unlike Westpac, a cardholder’s cover will depend on when the insurable event takes place rather than when the customer booked their travel. Any travel after the change date will be under ANZ’s new policy structure.
NAB It made significant travel insurance changes in May, including axing international, domestic travel and rental car excess insurance for certain cards, and introduced lower cover limits for other cards in July 2025.
NAB also made changes to insurance for travel delay expenses, and some cards reduced international cover from up to three months to up to 30 consecutive days.
What about Amex?
Travel insurance through American Express cards, which are popular with frequent flyers and were among a handful of policies that paid out claims in the pandemic, has not yet been altered.
“There are no changes to announce at this time. We continue to evaluate the implications of these regulatory changes for our products,” an American Express spokeswoman said, and noted that insurance and rewards remained part of Amex’s commitment to value for card members.
The bottom line Australian Travel Industry Association chief executive Dean Long says he does not have a good opinion of the free travel insurance provided by credit cards.
“We always say you should be purchasing your insurance independent of your payment choice,” Long says.
“If you have a comprehensive policy, fit for purpose for your trip, either purchased with the insurance company direct or through a travel agent, you’re going to get a better result.
“There was always a level of confusion for consumers about how you activate it. There’s been a limited understanding of that insurance product to begin with, and now there will be a chance that consumers may think they are covered and they’re not.” Long says there is mass confusion among consumers about the Reserve Bank credit card changes, and he does not expect people to get clarity for another six months.
He says while credit card travel insurance should be ignored, proper policies are vital.
“If you can’t afford travel insurance, you can’t afford to travel,” Long says. “The minute something goes wrong, if you sprain your ankle, automatically you could be up for a hospital fee more than the entire cost of the holiday. A course of antibiotics in the US is almost worth more than a flight.”
